exercise1.prompt: a comment about pip install, and a function standing in for requests.get

cases.name: the code runs and prints something
there is a function standing in for the request

exercise1.hint: Two halves: a comment saying what pip install does, and a function you write yourself that pretends to fetch something. The comment is prose; the function has to be real code.

exercise2.prompt: comments for pip install and pip uninstall, then an explanation
exercise2.hint: One comment per command, then a print that says in your own words what pip is for.

questions.prompt: Where does `pip install requests` get the package from?
questions.explain: pip downloads from PyPI by default. That is the difference between a third-party package and a standard library module: one has to be fetched, the other is already there.

questions.prompt: Match each pip command to what it does.
right: Prints the version and location of one package
questions.explain: pip is a package manager, so its commands are the four things you do to a package: add it, see what you have, remove it, and inspect one.

questions.prompt: You ran `pip install requests`. What do you write in your Python file?
questions.explain: pip is a command you run in the terminal, once. Inside Python the package is imported like any other module.

questions.prompt: Which of these are true about third-party packages?
choices: They have to be installed before they can be imported
They are written and maintained by people outside the Python core team
A project should record which ones it needs
They are automatically available to every Python program on the machine
questions.explain: The last one is the trap. What is installed depends on which environment you are in, which is exactly the problem the next lesson is about.
